blocks.body: A frequency is where you listen. A mode is how the information rides on the radio signal. Voice, CW, and data can share the same idea of a tuned frequency and still be different signals. This bench is an educational model, not a waveform from a real radio.

config.intro: EDUCATIONAL MODEL. Set the receiver for the signal you are given. The tuned frequency stays the same.
config.doneText: Each signal needed its own receiver mode. Tuning to the frequency was not enough.

signals.info: Someone is speaking. The RF frequency is shifting with the voice.
Someone is speaking on a single sideband. It will not sound like FM.
A carrier is being keyed on and off. There is no voice.
A device is sending data tones. A speaker will not turn them into a conversation.

blocks.body: A signal is not an infinitely thin line on a chart. Different emissions occupy different amounts of spectrum. The bars below are a comparison inside an educational model. They are not universal bandwidth numbers and they are not a band plan.

config.intro: EDUCATIONAL MODEL. Which of these two signals occupies more spectrum in the model?
config.doneText: In this model the FM voice is wider than the CW signal. Real emissions vary.

choices.label: FM voice occupies more
choices.why: The FM voice bar is wider. Occupied bandwidth is the slice of spectrum the emission uses.

choices.label: CW occupies more
choices.why: CW is the narrower of these two in the model. A signal still has some width. It is just less.

blocks.body: Digital activity still uses a radio. A computer or other device does not replace the RF path. APRS, at this level, is station, location, or status data in packets carried by radio. It is not the same thing as an ordinary internet message.

config.intro: Build the digital path in order. This is the idea behind a future DigiRig or Waypoint Deck. No hardware is connected.
config.wrong: Keep the information moving toward RF, then back out at the far end.
config.doneText: The packet rode a radio path. It was not an internet message.

steps.label: COMPUTER / DEVICE
steps.note: The information starts in a device.

steps.label: AUDIO OR DATA INTERFACE
steps.note: The interface hands that information to the radio.

steps.label: RADIO
steps.note: The radio puts it on an RF signal.

steps.label: RF
steps.note: The signal travels as radio, not as a network cable.

steps.label: RECEIVING RADIO
steps.note: Another station's radio recovers the RF.

steps.label: DECODER / DEVICE
steps.note: A decoder turns it back into data the operator can use.

followUp.prompt: An APRS packet on this path says a station's location and a short status. What is it?

choices.label: Station data carried by radio
choices.why: APRS here is a packet of station, location, or status data. The radio is the transport.

choices.label: A normal internet text message
choices.why: The path you built never left the radio chain. Internet messaging is a different system.

blocks.body: Use the same ideas on a new signal, a satellite pass, and a direction-finding check. The satellite picture is a pass between two ground stations. It is not an orbit calculator.

config.intro: Ground station A transmits up. The satellite repeats. Ground station B listens. Line of sight has to exist during the pass.
config.doneText: Uplink, downlink, and the pass are three different ideas.

scenes.prompt: Which name is the signal going from your radio up to the satellite?

choices.label: Uplink
choices.why: Uplink is the transmission the satellite receives.

choices.label: Downlink
choices.why: Downlink is the signal coming back down from the satellite.

scenes.prompt: Which name is the signal your radio hears from the satellite?

choices.label: Downlink
choices.why: Downlink is what the ground station receives.

choices.label: Uplink
choices.why: Uplink already left the ground. You are listening to the return signal.

scenes.prompt: The satellite is only usable for a few minutes, and the tone seems to creep. What is a fair beginner statement?

choices.label: It is a pass, in line of sight, and the frequency can shift
choices.why: A pass is the usable window. Line of sight matters. Doppler is the idea that the frequency can change during that window.

choices.label: The satellite stays on one fixed frequency for the whole day
choices.why: This lab does not treat the frequency as locked for the pass.

config.doneText: You matched the mode, compared width, and treated direction finding as aiming a receiver.

scenes.prompt: You hear keyed tones, not a voice, on a frequency you know is in use. The radio is set to FM voice. What is wrong?

choices.label: The receiver mode does not match the signal
choices.why: Frequency selection found the signal. The mode still has to fit it.

choices.label: The frequency must be wrong because you cannot understand it
choices.why: A wrong mode can make a correctly tuned signal unreadable.

scenes.prompt: Three activities are offered: a voice net, a CW practice contact, and a data exchange. Which one is the data activity?

choices.label: The data exchange
choices.why: Data is information for a device. Voice and CW are different activities.

choices.label: The voice net, because the microphone is digital inside the radio
choices.why: A voice net is still voice, even if the radio has digital parts.

scenes.prompt: You are asked which way a hidden transmitter is. You rotate a directional antenna until the signal peaks.

choices.label: That is a simple direction-finding check
choices.why: Radio direction finding uses the signal itself to estimate a bearing. This is the beginner version, not a contest.

choices.label: That is an APRS packet
choices.why: Turning an antenna to peak a signal is not the same as sending a location packet.

blocks.prompt: Why isn't selecting the correct frequency always enough to understand a radio signal?
blocks.reference: The receiver has to be set for the kind of signal. FM voice, SSB voice, CW, and digital data put information on RF in different ways, and they can occupy different amounts of spectrum. A satellite downlink can also shift during a pass. Frequency finds where to listen. Mode and the receiver setup decide whether the information comes back out.
blocks.unsure: Think about the bench. The frequency stayed put while the signal changed from voice to CW to data. Only the matching receiver mode recovered it.

blocks.body: RADIO LAB PRACTICE. These questions are about the signals you just configured. They are not official exam questions.

blocks.label: RADIO LAB PRACTICE
blocks.notice: Original practice about modes, bandwidth, data, and a satellite pass. Not official exam questions.

questions.stem: You are tuned to the right frequency and still cannot understand the signal. What else does this lab require?
choices: A receiver mode that matches the emission
questions.why: Volume can make a matched signal easier to hear. It does not turn CW or data into the mode the receiver is set for.

questions.stem: In this lab's educational model, how should you think about occupied bandwidth?
choices: Every emission is an infinitely thin line at the center frequency
Different emissions can occupy different amounts of spectrum
Bandwidth is the same number for every mode
questions.why: The bars compared width. They were not a universal specification, and they were not zero-width lines.

questions.stem: Which activity in the bench was on-off keying rather than voice?
questions.why: CW keyed the carrier. FM and SSB were voice signals with different receiver settings.

questions.stem: Where does a beginner's digital message go between the two devices?
choices: Computer, interface, radio, RF, receiving radio, decoder
Computer, internet router, website, other computer
questions.why: The path you assembled stays on radio. The interface and the radios are required.

questions.stem: What is APRS in this lab?
choices: Packets of station, location, or status data carried by radio
A voice net on a repeater
questions.why: APRS was introduced as radio transport for station data, not as a chat app and not as voice.

questions.stem: During a simple satellite contact, which signal does your radio transmit?
questions.why: Uplink goes to the satellite. Downlink is what you receive. The picture was one pass, not an orbit model.

questions.stem: You rotate a directional antenna until a signal peaks. What activity is that closest to?
choices: Choosing an FM voice receiver mode
questions.why: Direction finding uses the received signal to estimate where it is coming from. This lab does not turn that into a contest or a grid exchange.

blocks.body: Plan a portable outing that includes voice, an APRS or data check, and a simplified satellite pass. No radio is required. Choose the setup that matches each activity.

config.doneText: The plan has a voice mode, a radio data path, and a satellite uplink and downlink. That is a plan, not a contact.

scenes.prompt: The voice plan is a local FM net.

choices.label: Set the radio for FM voice and listen before calling
choices.why: The activity is voice, and the receiver mode has to match.

choices.label: Leave the radio in CW because the frequency is correct
choices.why: A correct frequency with the wrong mode will not produce the net.

scenes.prompt: You want a location and status packet to leave the station.

choices.label: Use a device, an interface, and the radio to send the packet
choices.why: APRS or other data still follows the radio path.

choices.label: Send a phone text and call it APRS
choices.why: A phone text is not the radio packet from this lab.

scenes.prompt: A satellite will be in view for a few minutes.

choices.label: Plan an uplink, a downlink, and a short pass while it is in line of sight
choices.why: You need both directions and the usable window. Expect the frequency idea to shift.

choices.label: Leave the antenna indoors and use yesterday's FM net frequency all afternoon
choices.why: A satellite pass is line of sight and uses its own uplink and downlink.
